title: 389. The HR experts just lost an HR lawsuit (and why it matters to you) 2026
author: Jeff Matlow
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever (thebestleadershipnewsletter.com), September 21,
summary: Jeff Matlow opens on the irony that SHRM, the world's largest HR association and the body that certifies HR professionals, lost an $11.5 million racial discrimination and retaliation verdict over its own employment practices. He then deliberately drops the case. What interests him is the mechanism alleged to have preceded it, and he walks the reader through two named research findings. Tokenism research holds that an underrepresented person becomes hyper visible, which invites closer watching. Joan C. Williams's Prove-It-Again Bias holds that women and people of color must supply more evidence of competence while others are judged on potential. Matlow's contribution is to connect the two into an accounting problem: unequal attention produces unequal documentation, so after six months one employee has a file of minor incidents while everyone else has a clean record, and the file looks objective from outside. His closing test is deliberately uncomfortable, asking managers to name the last small mistake each team member made and to notice if only one name comes to mind.
points: The piece's real subject is documentation rather than discrimination, arguing that a fair-looking evidence file can be the artifact of unfair observation.
Matlow explicitly decouples the mechanism from intent, noting a manager need not be consciously biased to simply watch the one different person more closely.
Confirmation bias is cast as the accelerant, since suspicion of underperformance makes the brain efficient at collecting proof of it.
The self-test he offers is behavioral rather than attitudinal, measuring where attention went rather than what the manager believes about themselves.
The postscript sharpens the institutional point: SHRM's own HR department held five meetings on the complaint and resolved nothing.
quotes: SHRM positions itself as the central authority on HR best practices. They certify HR professionals and teach companies how to manage employees. They create standards that everyone else is supposed to follow.

According to Rehab, her supervisor began treating her differently from her white colleagues. She was cut out of meetings she had previously attended. Her work was more closely watched and got stricter scrutiny.

Research on tokenism has found that people who are underrepresented within a group can become hyper visible. Their behavior attracts more attention, their differences are more exaggerated and their performance can get greater scrutiny.

That doesn’t mean the manager is consciously racist, sexist, ageist or any other -ist. Heck, that manager may not even be doing any of it consciously. They just naturally pay a little more attention to the one person who is different.
When you pay attention to everyone equally, you’ll notice some of everyone’s mistakes. Most are corrected and quickly forgotten. They don’t matter in the long scope of things.
Somewhere in here, confirmation bias joins the party. Because once you suspect that someone isn’t meeting your expectations, your brain is really good at finding the evidence to prove you’re right.

Williams’ research found that women and people of color are often required to provide more evidence of their competence than their colleagues. Other employees are more likely to receive the benefit of the doubt, or to be judged on their potential rather than their actions.

Can you name, off the top of your head, the last small mistake each person made? Not the catastrophic ones. I’m talking about the small, forgettable ones. The typos. Missed deadlines. Showing up late. That type of thing.
